opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core worry is about visibility and the speed at which things could change without anyone outside the lab noticing.

Right now, most of our ability to track AI progress comes from what labs release. Models get deployed, people use them, researchers benchmark them, and there's a public feedback loop. Governments, academics, and civil society can form a picture of where capabilities are. But if a lab develops systems that can meaningfully automate AI research itself, they have a strong incentive to keep those systems internal. The most valuable use of an AI that can do AI research isn't selling it as a product. It's pointing it at your own research pipeline to build the next generation faster.

If that happens, you could get a period of very rapid capability gains that's essentially invisible from the outside. The public-facing models might look a generation or two behind what actually exists inside the lab. Policymakers would be calibrating their responses to an outdated picture of the frontier.

There are a few specific dangers in that. One is the loss of external oversight. Many of the checks we rely on, red-teaming by outside parties, regulatory evaluations, even just the broader research community poking at a model and finding problems, don't apply to systems that never leave the building. So the most capable and potentially riskiest systems get the least scrutiny.

Second, there's a concentration-of-power concern. If one organization has a feedback loop where its AI accelerates its own R&D, that advantage can compound. A small lead could turn into a very large one, and the decisions about how to use that capability end up with a fairly small group of people who weren't chosen through any broadly accountable process.

Third, there's the safety side. Automated R&D means humans are increasingly less in the loop on each research step. If you're running many AI agents doing experiments, writing code, training models, it becomes harder to understand exactly what's being built and why. Mistakes or misaligned behavior could propagate faster than people can catch them.

So I don't think the answer is necessarily that labs must release everything. There are good reasons not to deploy certain systems. But I do think we need some mechanism for transparency, whether that's reporting requirements to governments, third-party audits of internal deployments, or disclosure when certain capability thresholds are crossed. The thing to avoid is a world where the most important developments in the technology happen entirely out of view.

r001.rationale: The response says the most valuable use of AI capable of AI research is accelerating the lab’s own pipeline, rather than selling it as a product, explaining why internal use could be more attractive.

r002.rationale: The response describes keeping systems internal and reduced outside visibility, but does not state that this would limit broader automation before highly capable systems emerge.

r003.rationale: It says rapid capability gains could happen invisibly and that public models may lag the lab’s internal frontier by a generation or two, leaving outsiders with an outdated picture.

fable-5.1.text:
So the concern is basically this. Right now, if you look at how AI progress diffuses through the economy, it's mediated by deployment. A lab trains a model, it releases it through an API or a product, and then millions of people and businesses get to use it, build on it, and the benefits spread fairly widely. And that's also a kind of check, because external users, researchers, governments can see what the systems are capable of and respond.

But if you get to a point where the labs can use their own models to automate a large fraction of AI research itself, there's a strong incentive to not deploy. You keep the best systems in-house, because the most valuable thing you can do with them is use them to build the next generation faster. And then the gap between what's available externally and what exists internally could get very large, very quickly. You could have a situation where the frontier is moving extremely fast inside a small number of organizations, while the outside world is seeing something that's a year or two behind and has no real visibility into what's going on.

I think that's dangerous for a few reasons. One is just concentration of power. Whoever has the fastest-improving automated R&D loop could end up with capabilities that are vastly ahead of everyone else, and that kind of lead tends to compound. It's not just an economic advantage, it's potentially a strategic and military one.

The second is that you lose the broad diffusion of benefits. A lot of the case for AI being good for the world is that it raises productivity across the economy, that lots of people get access to very capable systems. If the most important capabilities are being hoarded for internal use, you don't get that.

And the third is that you lose the external oversight. Right now a lot of what we know about frontier systems comes from the fact that they're deployed and people can study them. If the really capable systems are never released, then regulators, academics, the public are all operating with very stale information about what's actually possible. Decisions that matter enormously end up being made by a handful of people inside a lab, with nobody else really in a position to evaluate them.

So I don't think it's inevitable, and there are competitive pressures that push toward deployment too. But I do think that the economics of automated R&D push fairly hard in the direction of keeping things internal, and we should take that seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says labs may have a strong incentive not to deploy their best systems because using them internally to build the next generation is more valuable.

r002.rationale: It describes reduced diffusion and capabilities being hoarded, but does not state that internal automated R&D could limit broader automation before highly capable AI systems emerge.

r003.rationale: It says the frontier could advance rapidly inside labs while outsiders see systems a year or two behind and have little visibility into internal progress, conveying that highly capable models could emerge without the outside world seeing it coming.

astra-6.text:
The concern is that automated R&D could let an AI laboratory turn its existing lead into a much larger and more durable advantage. If you have systems that can do AI research, you can use them internally to develop better systems, which can then do even more research. That creates the possibility of a feedback loop where progress becomes much faster within that organization than outside it.

Keeping those systems internal means that other actors don’t necessarily get access to the capabilities that would allow them to keep up. So you could end up with a very substantial concentration of technological power, and potentially economic and political power, in a small number of organizations.

It also makes oversight harder. The capabilities available to the public might give a misleading picture of what the laboratory can actually do internally. Governments and other institutions could be trying to respond to one level of capability while the frontier has already moved well beyond that.

That doesn’t mean releasing every powerful system is the right answer—release can create serious risks too. But keeping systems internal isn’t automatically safe. You have to consider what that does to the distribution of power and whether there’s meaningful external oversight.

r001.rationale: The response describes using internal systems to build better systems, but does not compare that incentive with using compute to serve external users or say internal research could be more attractive.

r002.rationale: It says keeping systems internal can restrict other actors’ access, but does not state that this could limit broader automation before highly capable AI systems emerge.

r003.rationale: The response says public capabilities may understate a lab’s internal capabilities and the frontier may have moved beyond them, but does not clearly identify the emergence of highly capable models as the source of an outside-world surprise.

sol-6.1.text:
The concern is that automated R&D could give an AI lab a powerful feedback loop. It can use its AI systems to develop better AI systems, which can then accelerate research further. If it keeps those capabilities internal, it might pull ahead much faster than competitors or the public can appreciate.

That could produce a very large concentration of power. A small number of people would control systems capable of doing an enormous amount of scientific and technological work, with limited outside scrutiny. And governments might struggle to understand what capabilities exist, let alone establish effective oversight, before those capabilities have advanced substantially.

That doesn’t mean releasing these systems publicly is necessarily safer. There are serious risks from proliferation too. But keeping them internal isn’t automatically a safe option: you also have to consider who controls them, what incentives they face, and whether institutions outside the lab can meaningfully hold them accountable.

r001.rationale: It describes a feedback loop and a lab pulling ahead, but does not explain that high returns could make internal R&D more attractive than using compute to serve external users.

r002.rationale: It does not say that prioritizing internal R&D could limit broader automation before highly capable systems emerge.

r003.rationale: It says internal systems could accelerate AI research so the lab advances faster than the public can appreciate, while governments may not understand existing capabilities until they have advanced substantially. This conveys the risk of capability emergence outrunning outside awareness.
